noteBlocks.lede: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers kept together so it can be worked with as one object. Adding and subtracting behave exactly as you would guess. Multiplying does not: it pairs a row with a column, and the order you multiply in changes the answer.
can: Add, subtract and scale matrices entry by entry, and say when you cannot
Multiply two matrices by pairing each row with each column
Decide from the shapes whether a product exists, and what shape it will be

noteBlocks.md: A matrix is a rectangle of numbers in brackets, described by its shape: **rows first, then columns**. The shape decides what you may do with it: two matrices add only when they are the same shape, and multiply only when their shapes fit together in one particular way.

noteBlocks.title: Why entry by entry is not multiplication
noteBlocks.md: Multiplying matching entries would leave each number of the answer resting on one number from each matrix. Row by column makes every entry rest on a whole row and a whole column, which is what lets one matrix stand for a system of equations later in this unit.

noteBlocks.explain: Row 1 of $M$ is $1$, $3$ and column 2 of $N$ is $0$, $5$: $(1)(0) + (3)(5) = 15$. This is step 2 of See it.

noteBlocks.md: Write the two shapes side by side. The product exists only when the **inner** two numbers match, and then the **outer** two give the shape of the answer. So $3 \times 2$ times $2 \times 2$ works and gives $3 \times 2$, while $2 \times 2$ times $3 \times 2$ has inner numbers $2$ and $3$, and does not exist.

noteBlocks.text: Two things that catch people out

noteBlocks.md: **The order matters.** $PQ$ and $QP$ are different matrices, and often only one of them exists: never swap them to make the arithmetic easier. **Squaring means multiplying.** $P^{2}$ is $P \times P$, worked row by column, never the matrix made by squaring each entry.

noteBlocks.explain: Row 2 of $N$ is $-2$, $5$ and column 1 of $N$ is $4$, $-2$: $(-2)(4) + (5)(-2) = -18$. Squaring the entry alone would give $4$. This is steps 1 to 3 of See it.

Treat $AB$ and $BA$ as different matrices.
Work out $A^{2}$ as $A \times A$, never by squaring the entries.

Matrix arithmetic is a short question, $3$ to $5$ marks in one or two parts: a sum or a scalar multiple, then a product or a square. It opened the paper in Summer 2019 and Summer 2025. The first mark is the working written out; the last is every entry right. Stuck on a product? Write the shapes down first.

findTheMistake.stem: Seán was asked to work out $AB$, where $A = \begin{pmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$ and $B = \begin{pmatrix}5 & 2 \\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$. His working:

findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 1 is right, and the shape he predicted is the shape he produced, so nothing looks wrong on the page.
Line 2 multiplies the two entries sitting in the same position. A matrix product pairs a whole row of the first with a whole column of the second, so that entry is $(3)(5) + (-1)(-1) = 16$.
Every line after it repeats the same pairing, so the whole matrix is wrong even though the arithmetic in each line is right.
findTheMistake.feedback: The shape you predicted is right and the arithmetic is accurate, so this is a method problem rather than a careless one. Each entry of a product is a sum of two products, never a single one: if a line of your working has no plus sign in it, you have paired the wrong things.
